item.title: New parliamentary panel at #IGF2020.
item.description: As part of the 2020 Internet Governance Forum, the parliamentary roundtable took place on November 10. The topic discussed during the session was “Building Trust in the Time of the COVID-19 Response and Post-COVID-19 Recovery” (Parliamentary Roundtable: Building trust in a time of COVID-19 response and post-COVID-19 recovery - own translation -). During the meeting, a draft resolution prepared by DESA, the IPU, and the IGF Secretariat in collaboration with the 2019 and 2020 IGF hosts (Germany and Poland) was presented and opened for comment. Here you can view the list of registered parliamentarians. This draft is based on and builds upon the document titled Jimmy Schulz Call (1), drafted by the first group of parliamentarians representing 56 countries at the 2019 IGF. That document included a series of recommendations addressed to national parliaments. This year’s document notes that the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical role the Internet plays in sustaining basic economic processes, social interactions, and a minimum level of cultural life in the face of isolation. Now more than ever, it is necessary to guarantee Internet access, promote sound digital policies, strengthen multisectoral Internet governance, and foster trust in public officials and information. Furthermore, it emphasizes the responsibility that parliamentarians have to actively contribute to creating regulatory frameworks that promote an accessible, open, and secure Internet for users of this generation and future generations. It also highlights the need to address the gender gap and the digital divide so that everyone can reap the enormous benefits that digital technologies offer for sustainable development. It also mentions the drawbacks that the “infodemic” (a term coined by the WHO) on social media has caused in the fight against the pandemic and the importance of addressing the problem of misinformation from a systemic perspective rather than a purely legislative one. Finally, the document expresses the need to promote the active participation of parliamentarians in three distinct areas: Public Trust in the Internet Parliaments play a key role in helping to improve public trust in the Internet by:

item.title: Guatemala: The Temptation to Use the State of Emergency to Silence Critics and Criminalize "Fake News"
item.description: Guatemala: The Temptation to Use the Emergency to Silence Critics and Criminalize “Fake News” It is clear that extraordinary circumstances, such as a pandemic, call for extraordinary measures. And declarations of constitutional states of emergency—such as so-called states of alarm or emergency—are of that nature, or at least should be considered as such. In the specific case of Guatemala, the constitutional state of exception adopted is known as a state of public calamity (the specific effects of which took effect on March 17, 2020). It is true that both the universal system for the protection of human rights contained, among others, in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, Art. 4), as well as the inter-American system—developed primarily through the American Convention on Human Rights (ACHR, Art. 27), permit so-called temporary and proportionate “states of emergency,” but it is important to clarify that these in no way imply discretion in the exercise of power to act outside the law, much less without any oversight whatsoever. As Joaquín Urías rightly points out, “_The most bizarre and, at the same time, most dangerous provisions of the Constitution are those that provide for the possibility of suspending the constitutional order. They are often justified under the guise of ‘defending the Constitution’ through an ideological sleight of hand—namely, the notion that sometimes the Constitution must suspend its own application to defend itself against a threat. Behind this line of reasoning lies, for many, the suspicion—or the conviction—that democracy is not the best system for dealing with a crisis. This nostalgia for dictatorships is a simplistic approach.” _(Blog Al Revés y al Derecho, “State of Emergency and Limitation of Rights: Neither Exception Nor Suspension,” April 14, 2020). This quote is particularly relevant given that in several countries in Latin America—or rather, across the Americas—we have seen precisely how a longing for dictatorship is surfacing. In Guatemala, certain actions by the president have already drawn the attention of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) and its Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression (RELE) (report dated April 18, 2020). For example, it has been reported that a group of journalists has publicly denounced being discredited by the President and other officials; they also reported that online channels for asking questions about the response to COVID-19 had been restricted. And beginning in April, presidential decrees regularly issued under the State of Public Calamity have included a warning to the media: “Pursuant to the Public Order Law, advertising agencies, media outlets, and broadcasters are required to avoid publications that may cause confusion or panic or exacerbate the situation, and to assume the responsibilities arising therefrom.” (“the warning,” hereinafter). The verb “avoid” used in this presidential provision entails an obligation of “not to act,” that is, it imposes a duty of omission, under penalty of incurring the corresponding legal liabilities, which may even be of a criminal nature (the offense of violating public health measures, Art. 305 of the Penal Code, for example). This warning against engaging in certain conduct (such as publishing a news story or an opinion that is alarming or causes confusion, for example) is a subtle threat to the free expression of thought and information which, for the reasons explained below, even amounts to a threat of prior censorship. But before that, it seems relevant to mention some “constitutional curiosities or paradoxes.” The Political Constitution of the Republic of Guatemala (CPRG) allows for the temporary limitation of certain, very narrowly defined constitutional rights (Art. 138). Among the eight (8) rights included, the first paragraph of Article 35 of said Constitution—which is the article recognizing the freedom of expression—is expressly listed. However, the first paragraph of the aforementioned Article 35 itself establishes the following: “Freedom of expression is guaranteed through any means of dissemination, without censorship or prior licensing. This constitutional right may not be restricted by law or by any provision whatsoever”… (emphasis added). For its part, Guatemala’s Public Order Law (Decree No. 7)—a law dating from 1965 that provides a more comprehensive framework for declaring temporary states of constitutional emergency—contains an outdated provision in Article 35, which literally states: “For the duration of any state of emergency, media outlets are required to avoid publications that may cause confusion or panic or aggravate the situation. In such cases, as well as if they report on the circumstances in a biased manner, the editor-in-chief shall be reprimanded by the respective authority; and in the event of a repeat offense, prior censorship may be imposed on the media outlet in question.” For some constitutional scholars, there is a possibility of contradictions within the Constitution itself—that is, potential constitutional antinomies. Could it be argued that there is an antinomy in the CPRG in that it both permits the restriction of freedom of expression in cases of constitutional exception (Art. 138) and the constitutional declaration that such freedom cannot be restricted by any law or provision (Art. 35), without making any exceptions? If this answer is interpreted under the “pro hominem” principle and, furthermore, in accordance with the guidelines that the Inter-American Court of Human Rights has established regarding freedom of expression, then the impossibility of imposing any restrictions on that freedom should prevail, and therefore freedom of expression should not be one of the fundamental rights that can be temporarily and proportionately limited or suspended during a state of alarm or calamity. And if the position that freedom of expression cannot be limited in any way—much less through systems of censorship—is indeed upheld, then another curious fact emerges: the unconstitutionality of a provision contained in a law of constitutional rank. I am referring to the complete incompatibility of Article 35 of the Public Order Law with the system for the protection of human rights. Finally, the warning contained in the presidential provisions—highlighted in bold at the beginning, and which was evidently “inspired” by Article 35 of the Public Order Law—did not go so far as to explicitly warn of the imposition of prior censorship in an open and explicit manner, since this is the very least that a President and his advisors must know in the 21st century: that any form of prior censorship is strictly prohibited under the international system for the protection of human rights—a prohibition that has become binding constitutional law in Guatemala as a result, not only the relevant rulings of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights but also rulings by the country’s own Constitutional Court, which have established case law to that effect. However, the warning still encourages a form of censorship—self-censorship—by suggesting that publishing or commenting on news that could cause confusion may lead to legal proceedings against those who produce or disseminate it, in order to determine liability (which, as already mentioned, can extend to criminal charges). If Guatemala were a country—like a few others in Latin America—that had an adequate social security and public health system, perhaps the events themselves, as news stories, would not be so alarming. If there were a commitment to transparency, accountability, and the proper handling of data during a pandemic, perhaps the government itself would not be causing so much confusion with the information it provides. But the systemic failure of the country’s public health system is already becoming apparent, as is the authorities’ limited or nonexistent capacity to manage the crisis and disseminate information properly, along with the additional underlying conditions that make Guatemala a country particularly vulnerable to the pandemic. Publishing any news story that reflects our chronic institutional weakness—especially in public health—and the government’s incompetence, which exacerbates the situation (and is further compounded by possible cases of corruption), thus becomes a story that can cause confusion for anyone even moderately concerned about what is happening. Hence, a “threat” could come from some government entity instructing a media outlet to refrain from continuing to publish stories such as those that have appeared in its coverage, under penalty of legal consequences for failing to do so. The President, so far, has not exercised this “power,” despite or notwithstanding his warning (it is well known that the President does not have a natural affinity for journalists). There is one known isolated case involving the former Presidential Communications Secretary, who warned a radio station that a news story it had broadcast was alarmist and false and publicly reprimanded the station (Sonora), promptly deleting the critical tweet. By Álvaro Castellanos Howell Photo Credit: @mpbasham

item.title: Putting it in context: Zuckerberg’s publishing company, the Twitter-Trump conflict, and the responsibility of intermediaries in the face of long-standing social problems
item.description: On Thursday, June 18, the Clarín newspaper republished an op-ed by Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO of Facebook, originally published in USA Today the previous day, regarding measures taken by the company ahead of the upcoming U.S. presidential election. The editorial announced the creation of a space dedicated to political and election-related information on the Facebook and Instagram platforms, aimed at promoting better access to information and combating misinformation during election periods; and it commits to promoting and encouraging political participation as part of the company’s civic responsibility, in an effort to combat efforts aimed at voter suppression—a current debate in the U.S. from which Zuckerberg has not been exempt. These measures are not the first the company has taken regarding elections or misinformation; however, they come amid a complex context for major social media platforms—particularly Facebook and Twitter—which have faced severe criticism for irregularities in the enforcement of their community standards and their policies regarding content or statements by politicians. On May 26, 2020, U.S. President Donald Trump used his Twitter and Facebook accounts to tell his supporters that voting by mail would be fraudulent. He claimed that ballot boxes could be stolen, fake ballots could be printed, and even signatures could be forged. Many users and NGOs criticized this type of content, accusing it of being part of efforts to suppress voting among certain sectors and of casting a cloud of doubt and uncertainty over the integrity of the electoral process from the outset. In a radical policy shift, Twitter decided to have fact-checkers review this content. As a result, a fact-check label was applied to the tweet. Twitter determined that President Trump’s claim had no factual basis and therefore also provided links to resources for further information on the topic. This was the first time Twitter applied a fact-check and a fact-check label to a post made by the U.S. President. It is not the first time, however, that the company has taken action against content created and disseminated by public officials—and even presidents of other countries—but it is the first time it has done so regarding content from the U.S. President, whose headquarters, coincidentally, are located there. Facebook, on the other hand, chose not to submit the post to its fact-checkers, arguing that when it comes to political expression, the company should not act as an arbiter of truth. The differing positions of the two companies are thus laid bare. At the same time, the tragic murder of George Floyd occurred, sparking public outrage, laying bare the inequalities and systematic discrimination that exist in the U.S. against the Black community, and triggering intense protests across the country and eventually around the world. Some of these protests led to looting, destruction of property, and violence. Faced with this situation, the President of the United States once again turned to his Twitter and Facebook accounts to warn the people of Minneapolis that if the state government failed to contain the situation, he would send in the National Guard. He concluded his statement with a particularly problematic phrase: “When looting starts, shooting starts.” The phrase is believed to have been taken from the Miami police chief, who in 1967 promised violent reprisals against those who protested the “stop-and-frisk” policies. Twitter determined that the President’s statements constituted incitement to violence, which violates Twitter’s terms and conditions of service, but that there was a journalistic interest in these statements because they came from the President of the United States. Consequently, it hid the content behind a warning that summarized the above. Zuckerberg, on the other hand, determined that the content in question was political in nature and that there was a general public interest in ensuring that such content was not hidden or blocked; he therefore chose to leave it on his platform as is, without any warning. Facebook publicly maintains that political speech—particularly that of public officials—is subject to high levels of scrutiny and is in the public interest. This argument aligns with what the company has been stating for months regarding political content, which, in theory, is exempt from external fact-checking and is generally considered to be of sufficient journalistic interest to be left up even if it violates its Community Standards. Criticism was once again swift to follow, even from within the company and among its own employees. Amid these discussions—which are nothing more than anecdotal, despite having already sparked reactions from the government and society—a fundamental question arises: How should these companies handle statements made by public officials on social media? What role do we, as citizens and users, want these platforms to play in our election campaigns? Or in the management of our emergencies? Or in our democracies in general? These are the questions that, despite the many revisions to terms and conditions of service and the numerous measures attempted, remain relevant and await a definitive answer. The measures announced by Zuckerberg this week are part of this broader and more fundamental debate. And unfortunately, while this commitment is a step in the right direction, it does not resolve these more structural issues. Just to give one example, on June 18, The Verge reported that Facebook removed nearly 80 paid ads from Trump from the platform because they contained images of an inverted triangle—a symbol used to identify political dissidents in Nazi concentration camps. And once again, we return to the fundamental question. It is imperative to clarify the criteria these companies—which have billions of users worldwide—apply to the speech of public officials on matters of public interest, and to provide even greater transparency regarding the implementation of community guidelines or terms and conditions of service. It is also urgent to clarify what we, as users—but above all as citizens—want these platforms to do with this type of content. It is urgent to promote a broad and informed debate on the repercussions these decisions have on our political systems and our democracies. This is the best contribution we can make to promote democracy, not only in the United States but globally. By Agustina Del Campo twitter.com/@agustinadelcamp

item.title: Facebook Under Scrutiny: Exceptions for Journalistic Interest and Political Speech
item.description:
Given the importance of issues such as freedom of expression, surveillance and privacy, policing, and private and public censorship at this particularly critical moment both globally and locally, we are republishing an article that we believe is relevant, insightful, and timely.

A More Permissive Stance Toward Political Speech In an interview in late September 2019, Nick Clegg, Facebook’s Vice President of Global Affairs and Communications, announced changes to the social network’s policies on speech moderation and exceptions based on journalistic value.
